title: Bidirectional Dijkstra on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing Bidirectional Dijkstra pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡ Inside high-scale navigation engines—watch the graph search split into two synchronized frontiers. One Dijkstra runs forward from the start, another runs backward from the goal, and when their settled regions touch, we reconstruct the shortest path.

🔧 Technical breakdown (visual):
• Forward frontier settles shortest distances from source
• Backward frontier settles shortest distances from target
• The stopping condition uses the best known meeting cost (min over explored overlaps)
• Fewer expanded nodes than classic Dijkstra on large road grids

✅ Takeaway: If your edges are non-negative, Bidirectional Dijkstra can dramatically cut work—especially when the start/goal are far apart.

🤔 Debate question: Do you think bidirectional search is always better, or should engineers choose direction-heuristics (A*/landmarks) when graph structure favors them?

fb_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra is a graph search upgrade for shortest paths: instead of exploring outward from only the start, it runs two Dijkstra searches—one forward from the source and one backward from the destination—until the frontiers meet. This often reduces the number of nodes expanded on large navigation graphs.
